newsitem.title: zaire: Militant opposition pressures Congo's Kabila.
newsitem.headline: Militant opposition pressures Congo's Kabila.

text.p: The militant opposition in Democratic Republic of Congo campaigned openly for a role in the new government promised by self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila for Thursday night.
Radical student supporters of populist opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi even threatened to take to the streets by Monday if their hero is not named prime minister.
As part of moves to choose his new team, Kabila set a much-awaited meeting with Tshisekedi, who has an army of fanatical supporters in the slums of Kinshasa.

Hundreds of militants have been virtually camping in solidarity outside Tshisekedi's home. Their leaders worked the crowd to a frenzy with speeches reminding Kabila that their own campaign paved the way for last Saturday's overthrow of dictator Mobutu Sese Seko by Kabila's AFDL alliance forces.
"We put Mobutu in a political ambulance and the AFDL took took him to the cemetery," declared Tshisekedi's close associate Joseph Olengankoy.

"Our allies (Kabila's forces) came into the capital because the path had already been prepared by our internal struggle. We were not afraid of Mobutu's tanks and so no other tanks will make us afraid," he told the cheering crowd.
A senior member of Kabila's guerrilla alliance which seized power in Kinshasa after a seven-month armed campaign said a new government would be announced on Thursday night.
"I will announce the composition of the government at 8.30 p.m. (1930 GMT) at the latest," Raphael Ghenda, the Alliance's information commissioner, told reporters.
Asked if Kabila had met or would meet Tshisekedi on Thursday, Ghenda replied: "I have no idea about that. I have just left the president (Kabila) and he was not with Mr Tshisekedi".
Ghenda said he did not know if Tshisekedi would be in the new government.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) captured Kinshasa on May 17 and controls almost all of Africa's third largest country, formerly Zaire. Mobutu is in exile, currently in Togo.
Earlier a Tshisekedi aide said Kabila and the radical leader were to meet on Thursday, but there was no sign of this happening.
Kabila's top aide met Tshisekedi on Wednesday for talks on forging a broad-based administration, as demanded by foreign governments.
Kabila arrived in Kinshasa on Tuesday from his Alliance's temporary headquarters in the southern city of Lubumbashi. He has been out of public view since, preparing his cabinet.
The United States, which joined South Africa in mediating in the Zaire conflict, has been working behind the scenes to bring the country's two strongmen together.
"We have a facilitating role. We are able to get in touch with both sides," U.S. embassy spokesman Joao Escodi told Reuters. "Now they have to do the talking. We're not involved in the talks."
Even if Tshisekedi is appointed prime minister, it is not clear what legal framework will guide his relations with Kabila and whether he will have executive powers.
Kabila scrapped Mobutu's transitional constitution and parliament.
Western powers have catiously voiced backing for Kabila, linking full recognition and economic aid to progress on broad-based democratic rule.
